name: Jaw contouring makeup (contour/highlight)

lead: Jaw contouring uses a darker shade to create shadow and a lighter shade to bring the edge forward, so the jawline looks more defined. It uses the same shading idea applied to cheekbones and noses.

The effect is optical: darker shades read as shadow and lighter shades as raised areas, changing perceived shape. It is visible as soon as it is blended and lasts until removed. The technique has a long theatrical and film history and went mainstream in the 2010s through celebrity and social media use.

paras: People blend a shade slightly darker than their skin under the jaw edge and a lighter shade along the edge, usually for photos, video or events, and remove it at the end of the day.
The sources consulted do not discuss risks; it is a temporary, cosmetic product application.

angle.text: A sharper-looking jawline on the spot. A darker shade creates shadow under the jaw and a highlight brings the edge forward. The effect shows as soon as it is blended and lasts until removed.

lead: Jaw contouring is the use of makeup shading and highlighting to make the jawline look sharper and more defined. A shade slightly darker than the skin is placed along and beneath the jaw to suggest shadow, a lighter shade is placed where the edge should catch light, and the two are blended so the lower face reads as more angular and the chin and neck separate more cleanly in photos and in person.[1][2]

The technique applies the general practice of contouring, in which darker shades recede and lighter ones advance. Contouring has a long theatrical and film history and became mainstream in the 2010s through celebrity and social media use.[1] It is temporary and cosmetic: the effect lasts until the makeup is removed, and it works as an optical illusion rather than changing bone or soft-tissue structure.

Brands and makeup artists present jaw contouring for both women and men. Men's grooming coverage in 2026 describes growing use of complexion products by straight men, with industry voices stressing subtle enhancement rather than heavy contouring.[3] Looksmaxxing forum threads discuss bronzer and contour as ways to change how a face is perceived without surgery.[4]
infobox: Contour and highlight powders, creams or sticks; bronzer

paras: General contouring places a darker shade in hollows or along edges to suggest shadow and a lighter shade on prominent areas; strobing uses lighter shades only.[1] Applied to the jaw, the same shading principle is used to suggest a sharper edge.

A beauty brand tutorial describes tilting the chin up, applying a medium-dark contour along the edge of the jaw, adding a second layer under the chin and along the jaw for depth, blending with a clean brush into the chin and cheekbones, and finishing with a highlighter along the jawline for contrast while avoiding the chin. The tutorial states the aim as a sculpted jawline that appears slimmer and more chiselled.[2] Cream products give a more emphasized look than powder, and setting spray is used to hold the result.[1][2]

Men's makeup coverage describes the aim as looking more defined and well-rested rather than visibly made up, and industry figures quoted in that coverage describe the growth as being in subtle products.[3]

Elizabethan actors used chalk and soot so that expressions could be read from a distance, and greasepaint replaced soot under electric stage lighting. Marlene Dietrich used shading in 1920s and 1930s films, and Max Factor Sr. added shading in 1934 so faces would not look flat on screen.[1] In 1945 Max Factor Sr. presented what Wikipedia describes as the first tutorial on contouring for different face shapes.[1] Kevyn Aucoin popularized a sculpted look in the 1990s, and his October 2000 book Face Forward is credited with introducing contouring to the public. In the 2010s, Kim Kardashian and others intensified the trend, and affordable brands made contour products widely available. Drag performers use contouring to emphasize or soften features.[1]

A looksmax.org thread titled around changing the entire face with bronzer, contour and fake tan reflects how some members treat makeup and tanning as quick tools for altering facial appearance.[4] Contouring is also discussed alongside non-temporary options such as jaw fillers and implants, which change real structure instead of shading it.
No studies found. A 2025 randomized trial compared facial roller and gua sha massage for facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity, which is a different intervention from makeup.[5]
